articles.body: Sites that start from a stock theme tend to look like it. This one did too — until recently it was the default PaperMod screen. The editorial homepage and unified article styling you're looking at came out of a single day of customization. This guide is that work written down, with the code. One principle drove all of it: never fork the theme. The theme stays a submodule and keeps receiving updates; you win with site-level files only. Hugo resolves same-path site files ahead of theme files, which makes this possible.

articles.title: Reading Karpathy's Lord of the Rings Demo: What Long Context Plus Autonomy Opens for Builders
articles.excerpt: A demo Andrej Karpathy posted over the weekend stuck with me. He gave Opus 5 a million-token context and the first paragraph of The Lord of the Rings, and asked for a procedural 3D rendering of the sc…
articles.body: A demo Andrej Karpathy posted over the weekend stuck with me. He gave Opus 5 a million-token context and the first paragraph of The Lord of the Rings, and asked for a procedural 3D rendering of the scene in Three.js. The model worked alone for about two hours, wrote 5,500 lines, and coordinated polygon placement, camera paths, and animation on its own. Total cost: about $10. The result is faster to watch than to describe. Most reactions read it as the next step past "draw a pelican SVG" benchmarks. Something else looked bigger to me. What changed isn't the model's artistry. It's the unit of delegation. The unit of delegation changed Until now, the work we handed agents came in prompt-sized pieces. One function, one bug, one file. Anything bigger, we decomposed ourselves.

articles.excerpt: Part of "AI, engineering and what survives production", a series on the parts of building with AI that hold up once real traffic hits them. There is a claim going round that you have probably absorbed…
articles.body: Part of "AI, engineering and what survives production", a series on the parts of building with AI that hold up once real traffic hits them. There is a claim going round that you have probably absorbed by now: AI-assisted development is making codebases worse. Refactoring is down, duplication is up, we are all writing more and revising less. The numbers behind it are real, the samples are enormous, and I found I had started repeating the conclusion in conversation without ever having checked it. Then it occurred to me that those figures are averages taken across hundreds of millions of changes from thousands of organisations, not one of which is mine. So what is the rate in your repository? Nobody has told you, and on current evidence nobody is going to.

articles.title: Fast... But Wrong? Meet Cache Invalidation
articles.excerpt: This is Part 7 of my "From One User to One Million" series, where we'll build an understanding of System Design by following a simple application as it grows from a single user to millions. Instead of…
articles.body: This is Part 7 of my "From One User to One Million" series, where we'll build an understanding of System Design by following a simple application as it grows from a single user to millions. Instead of memorising technologies, we'll learn why they exist by solving real problems as they appear. Last time, we ended on a question that sounded simple but isn't. Aisha updated her profile picture. Her new photo is now saved in the database. But the cache is still holding onto the old one, completely unaware that anything changed. So every request for Aisha's profile gets served the old data. Confidently. Instantly. Incorrectly. How does a cache know when the data it's holding is no longer correct? Think about what we've actually built at this point.

articles.excerpt: Introduction In June 2026, the IETF published RFC 10008 - the first new general-purpose HTTP method since PATCH was introduced in 2010. The method is called QUERY. In simple terms: QUERY = Safety of G…
articles.body: Introduction In June 2026, the IETF published RFC 10008 - the first new general-purpose HTTP method since PATCH was introduced in 2010. The method is called QUERY . In simple terms: QUERY = Safety of GET + Body of POST You can now send complex search/filter queries in the request body, while the server knows the operation is safe and idempotent . This means caching, automatic retries, and CDNs can all work properly. This single change can finally end the long-standing practice of using POST for search. The Problem We Had 1.

articles.title: Claude Code Subagents: Setup, Config, and When to Use Them
articles.excerpt: Most Claude Code sessions get slow and cluttered for the same reason: every exploratory grep, every log dump, and every "let me check one more file" stays in the main conversation forever. Subagents e…
articles.body: Most Claude Code sessions get slow and cluttered for the same reason: every exploratory grep, every log dump, and every "let me check one more file" stays in the main conversation forever. Subagents exist to fix exactly that problem. They are one of the agent primitives built into Claude Code for handling noisy, parallelizable work — a way to push the mess into an isolated window and bring back only the summary that matters. A subagent is not a smarter Claude, and it is not the same thing as a Skill. It is a separate reasoning agent with its own context window, its own tool allowlist, and no memory of your current conversation unless you explicitly fork it.

The software is polished, Gemini takes the hassle out of everyday tasks , and features like Magic Eraser, Best Take, and Call Notes have become so ingrained in my routine that I instantly miss them whenever I pick up another phone. articles.title: Star Wars the Ninth Jedi Review: a New Hope for the Franchise, from an Unexpected Source
articles.excerpt: The stylish, heartfelt show forges a bold path forward for a franchise struggling after the failure of The Mandalorian and Grogu
articles.body: It is a dark time for Star Wars . The Mandalorian and Grogu was a box office flop, earning less than the low-budget horror films Obsession and Backrooms – a failure that puts the franchise’s cinematic future in jeopardy. Ahsoka season 2 was postponed until 2027 and The Acolyte was canceled. Yet there is a new hope. The Ninth Jedi , an anime first developed by Production I.G. for the Star Wars: Visions anthology series, is exactly the sort of refresh Lucasfilm needed. The stylish, heartfelt series remixes the most iconic elements of Star Wars to create something that feels vital after decades of iterating on the Skywalker Saga.
articles.author: Sam Nelson

articles.title: Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi Season 1 Review
articles.excerpt: Despite some early growing pains, Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi is a terrific and excitingly unique take on the iconic franchise.
articles.body: This is a spoiler-free review of all eight episodes of Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi. The entire series is live now on Disney+ and Hulu. The Star Wars franchise is definitely in a bit of a slump lately. The Sequel Trilogy ended poorly, and Lucasfilm is still in the process of figuring out how to move forward in that era. Meanwhile, the mediocre performance of The Mandalorian and Grogu shows that even that once dependable pillar of the franchise is hemorrhaging support. But one thing fans can generally count on is that Star Wars will always deliver when it comes to new animated projects. Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi does nothing to change that fact.

articles.body: Ted Lasso Season 4 debuts August 5 on Apple TV . Three years after a Season 3 finale that sure did feel like a series finale at the time, Ted Lasso is back for a fourth season after all. In the modern streaming world, it’s become far too typical for a three-year gap between seasons to become something of a norm. At least Ted Lasso is accounting for this prolonged break in a bigger way, with a semi-reboot approach that feels more akin to a show being revived 10-15 years later rather than one we last saw the same year Oppenheimer was in movie theaters.

articles.title: X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 8 Review & Recap: "Dead Man's Hand"
articles.excerpt: X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 8 features a return fans have been waiting for, so why does it leave us feeling so cold? Read our full review of "Dead Man's Hand."
articles.body: Warning: This review contains full spoilers for X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 8! I have to wonder if it was the smartest idea for the X-Men '97 crew to telegraph the resurrection of Gambit (A.J. LoCascio). At the time, that stinger scene was a great way to cap off Season 1 and tease what was to come. But now that we've finally arrived at Season 2, is having that knowledge working against the show as it actually brings Gambit back into play? All I can say for sure is that something is missing in Episode 8. Gambit's resurrection doesn't pack quite the emotional punch his death did back in 2024. Maybe part of the problem is that we don't get a great sense of what Apocalypse's (Ross Marquand) larger goals are here.

articles.title: Total solar eclipse Aug. 12, 2026 live updates — 1 week to go
articles.excerpt: Follow our live coverage of the total solar eclipse 2026 as we count down to eclipse day with the latest news, expert insight and updates before bringing you live reports from Greenland and Spain.
articles.body: On Aug. 12, 2026, Europe will experience its first total solar eclipse since 1999, as the moon's shadow sweeps across Greenland, Iceland, northern Spain and the Balearic Islands. Along the narrow path of totality, day will briefly turn to twilight as the moon completely covers the sun, revealing its elusive outer atmosphere — the corona. Meanwhile, millions more skywatchers across much of Europe, as well as parts of northeastern United States and eastern Canada, will witness a partial solar eclipse as the moon appears to take a bite out of the sun. Live reporting from the path of totality We'll be following the eclipse from two locations along the path of totality.

articles.title: 1 week to go until a dramatic total solar eclipse darkens the skies over Spain, Iceland and Greenland
articles.excerpt: Here's what you need to know before the total solar eclipse one week from now.
articles.body: Get ready stargazers! We're just one week away from the total solar eclipse on Aug. 12, when millions of stargazers will be treated to a spectacular display as the lunar disk passes in front of the sun, blocking its light. Roughly 15.2 million people spread across Greenland, Iceland, Portugal, Russia and Spain will be in the path of totality during the total solar eclipse 2026 , where the moon will completely hide the sun's disk starting at 12:58 p.m. EDT (1658 GMT), according to Time and Date . A further 980 million people — approximately 12% of Earth's human population — will bear witness to a partial eclipse, as the lunar disk appears to takes a bite out of the sun.
